title: What would you expect from an AI-powered ASCII roguelike?
author: GulbrandrGameStudios
selftext:
I’ve been experimenting with a small ASCII roguelike prototype focused on procedural events, AI-generated interactions and terminal-style gameplay.

So far the game already has:

\- procedural world generation  
\- random events  
\- inventory system  
\- NPC quests  
\- a main objective for the player

It’s still very early, but I’m thinking about releasing a tiny playable demo soon.

What should I add before releasing a demo?

comments.author: ProjektProgram
comments.body: It would have to be lightspeed fast loading times for the art to actually appeal.

replies.author: GulbrandrGameStudios
replies.body: I only use AI for quests and descriptions. I’ve tried using it to make ASCII art but I don’t like the results:(

comments.author: No-Marionberry-772
comments.body:
are the quests and such generated by the llm?


ive got a project very similar to thia but getting it into a place where it does better than traditional generarive techniques has been a real challenge.

replies.author: GulbrandrGameStudios
replies.body: Good question. I’ve created a few base formulas for quests and item or enemy types. Once an event happens, the algorithm chooses a formula and sends an api prompt to create the quest text. Once that’s done, the algorithm chooses the most suitable item type as a reward and the api creates the item and its description. What do you think?

comments.author: oniris
comments.body: An extremely high number of races and classes. Also many interesting stats.

replies.author: GulbrandrGameStudios
replies.body: It’s a good plan for the future. For now, it only supports a lot of genres, like fantasy, northern gothic, pirates, etc:)

comments.author: Former_Produce1721
comments.body:
I have thought about this quite a lot, and have come to the conclusion that the best way to approach this is to have a deterministic game core that presents boring data, and use the AI to skin it.

Imagine Dwarf Fortress, but the descriptions and logs are re formulated by AI to be more flavorful and unique.

The reason I lean towards this is that AI by itself can not stay on track. It will always hallucinate or introduce inconsistencies.

I am making a roguelike right now and I set up tools and interfaces the AI can use, but never let it produce anything without going through a deterministic path. For example it can create JSON files to generate quests. It can use a CLI to play the quest and iterate on it. But it's never allowed to directly modify the domain. This is strictly protected by deterministic code.

replies.author: Former_Produce1721
replies.body:
Nice!

Did you have much success in getting it to build quests, play them, and iterate over them?

I have not found the secret sauce for this yet. It ends up always making really shitty quests haha

replies.author: GulbrandrGameStudios
replies.body:
For the current version, I use main quests like: character X should rescue character/object Y in location Z, which is guarded by enemy W.

And for NPC quests: You should defeat enemy X, which is located in terrain type Y. etc.

replies.author: Former_Produce1721
replies.body:
So you design these systematically and then let the AI skin it?

I've been thinking of something similar where each quest is a set of boring basic data building blocks and ai can assemble and skin them

replies.author: mallcopsarebastards
replies.body: you just need a validation stage. Let the AI go, then pass the result through a system that makes sure what it generated is interanlly consistent
